sources.title: Mollusca
sources.accessNote: Lead and anatomy summary read directly. A tertiary source: its figures cite primary literature, so claims built on it are marked moderate confidence.

sources.title: Mollusca (AphiaID 51)
sources.accessNote: Verified through the WoRMS REST record AphiaRecordByAphiaID/51: status accepted, rank Phylum, kingdom Animalia. MolluscaBase is the mollusc section of WoRMS.

claims.text: Molluscs form an accepted animal phylum, Mollusca, in the global register of marine species; the species names in this simulator follow the same register (WoRMS / MolluscaBase).
claims.evidenceNote: Machine-readable WoRMS record for AphiaID 51 returns status accepted and rank Phylum. Each species in the simulator carries its own AphiaID claim.

claims.text: About 86,600 living mollusc species are recognised, making molluscs the second-largest animal phylum. Gastropods, the snails, account for about 80% of classified mollusc species.
claims.evidenceNote: Figures read directly from the article lead, which cites its counts. Species counts change as new species are described, so these are approximate.

claims.text: A mollusc's soft body is mostly muscle. Its mantle encloses a cavity used for breathing and excretion and secretes the shell, which is made of proteins and chitin reinforced with calcium carbonate. Most molluscs feed with a rasping radula and move on a single muscular foot.
claims.evidenceNote: From the article's description of the features shared by modern molluscs and its 'hypothetical ancestral mollusc'. Individual groups vary: bivalves lack a radula and cephalopods have arms rather than a crawling foot.

claims.text: Nearly all molluscs lay eggs. Depending on the group, these hatch as trochophore larvae, as more complex veliger larvae, or as miniature adults.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from the article's overview of molluscan reproduction. Which route a species takes is given by its own sourced claims where known.
